newsitem.title: UK: Panama's first-ever Eurobond takes the hat - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Panama's first-ever Eurobond takes the hat - dealers.

text.p: Investors flocked to purchase Panama's first-ever Eurobond on Monday, enticed by the issue's high yield and reassured by recent Panamanian credit ratings.
"The deal was several times oversubscribed," Stephen DeSalvo, syndicate manager at BankBoston Corp, which was the lead manager for the bond said.
"We were able to double the issue size to $500 million."

The transaction, a $500 million 7.875 percent five-year Eurobond, was priced to yield 175 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasury notes. Immediately after the bond began to trade, the spread over U.S. Treasuries shrank 20 basis points, reflecting brisk demand for Panamanian paper.
DeSalvo said the bond was able to be sold at the tighter end of an expected 175-185 basis point range over U.S. Treasuries following an extensive marketing campaign in over 10 cities.
He said the deal saw over 100 geographically-diverse accounts buy the Eurobond.
"Around 11 percent of the deal sold to Asian accounts, 19 percent sold to Europe, 69 percent to U.S. accounts and one percent to Latin American institutional investors," he said.
"U.S. accounts were well-diversified between traditional emerging market buyers, high-yield accounts and high-grade funds."
The launch spread was the tightest spread for an inaugural public sector issue out of Latin America.
Emerging market syndicate managers in London said investor demand for new credits in the Latin American region was strong.
"The rating is good, the roadshows were successful and they could have launched the deal much tighter," a syndicate manager at a German bank said.
Another dealer at a U.S. house said: "It is a bought deal."
Dealers said the generously priced transaction would open up the international bond markets for Panamanian companies.

Panama -- a narrow republic linking north and south America -- was recently rated a sovereign ceiling rating of Ba1 by Moody's Investors Service and BB plus by Standard & Poor's Corp. Both ratings were at the high end of the "speculative grade" rating scale.

S&P said the outlook for the country was stable due to the strong political committment of the Perez Balladares government to deepen reforms, notably in the areas of privatisation and trade liberalization.
Moody's said the difference between the sovereign ceiling and the government's bond rating reflected the use of the U.S. dollar in Panama and the lack of foreign exchange controls.
In January Panama announced the proceeds of the Eurobond would be used to help pay off the nation's external debt.
